opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the biggest thing it revealed is that the collaboration looks very different from what people imagine. People picture typing in a problem and getting a proof back. That's not what happened.

The question was whether the iterates of Nesterov's method, not just the function values, actually converge for smooth convex functions. People in optimization have wondered about this for a long time, and I had tried it myself on and off without success. So I sat down with ChatGPT and worked through it over a few evenings, maybe twelve hours in total.

Most of what the model produced was wrong. It would propose an argument, and I'd spot a gap or an invalid step and push back. But what struck me was that among all those flawed attempts, it kept generating ideas, new Lyapunov-style quantities, different ways to combine inequalities, at a speed and breadth I couldn't match on my own. Some of those ideas were genuinely promising, even when the surrounding argument fell apart. My job became recognizing which threads were worth pulling on, steering it away from dead ends, and checking every step carefully.

So the lesson for me was about the division of labor. The model is an extraordinary explorer. It's tireless, it doesn't get discouraged, and it's willing to try things I might have dismissed too early. But it isn't yet a reliable verifier of its own work, and it doesn't always know when it's fooling itself. The human expert still has to supply judgment, taste, and rigor. When you put those together, though, you can move much faster than either could alone. For an open problem like this, I think that combination got us to the answer in days rather than what could easily have been much longer.

It also changed how I think about my own research. I now see these tools less as a calculator or search engine and more as a very energetic, sometimes overconfident, collaborator. You have to know how to work with that personality, but once you do, it's remarkably productive.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the honest answer is that it was more surprising than I expected, and also more mundane than people assume.

So the problem was a convergence question about Nesterov's accelerated gradient method, specifically whether the iterates themselves converge, not just the function values. That had been sitting open for a while. I'd thought about it on and off over the years and hadn't cracked it. When I started working through it with ChatGPT, the model didn't hand me a proof. I want to be very clear about that. What it did was act like a very fast, very well-read collaborator who never gets tired of trying one more thing.

The pattern was that I'd set up the structure, say "here's the Lyapunov function I think should work, here's where the argument breaks," and it would propose a modification, usually something wrong, occasionally something half-right. And the half-right ones were the valuable ones, because they'd push me to look at the problem from an angle I'd been avoiding. One of its suggestions pointed toward a technique I knew but hadn't connected to this problem, and that connection was the key step.

What it revealed to me is a few things. First, verification is the whole game. The model is confident whether it's right or wrong, so you have to check every line, and that checking is where the actual mathematics happens. Second, it's extremely good at breadth. It knows the literature in a way that I, in a narrow subfield, sometimes don't. Third, and this is the part I find genuinely interesting, the division of labor is strange. It wasn't doing the creative part and I wasn't doing the grunt work. It was more like a conversation where the ideas came out of the back-and-forth itself, and I'd be hard pressed to say who contributed what.

I think the real lesson is that this is a tool for mathematicians, not a replacement for them, at least right now. The judgment about what's a promising direction, what's actually true, what's worth writing down, that was still all on me. But the speed of iteration changed how I worked. I'd spend an hour on a dead end instead of a week. And that compounds.

astra-6.text:
It made me think of ChatGPT as a mathematical collaborator whose suggestions you still have to verify. With an open problem, you don’t know in advance which approach will work. A suggestion can be useful even if it isn’t a complete proof—it can give you a different way to formulate the question or point you toward an argument you hadn’t considered.

The crucial part is the back-and-forth: asking where an argument fails, identifying what remains to be shown, and checking each step carefully. You can’t substitute a convincing explanation for a correct proof. But you can use that interaction to expand the ideas you explore. That’s the potential I see for mathematical research.

sol-6.1.text:
It showed me that ChatGPT could be useful as a research collaborator even when it couldn’t solve the whole problem on its own. In mathematics, a suggestion can be valuable without being a complete proof—it might give you a different way to frame the question or an intermediate step worth exploring.

But you still have to check the reasoning carefully. A convincing explanation isn’t the same thing as a correct argument. For me, the productive approach was to stay actively involved: ask precise questions, challenge the answers, and work through the details. The value was in that back-and-forth.
